title: Design: Min Stack
oneLiner: A stack that can also tell you its smallest element at any moment, with every operation in O(1).
keyTakeaway: Store the minimum ALONGSIDE each element: when you push x, also record min(x, the min below it). The stack below an entry never changes while that entry is on top, so the min saved with it stays correct, and popping automatically restores the previous minimum.
explanation:
Build a stack with push(x), pop(), top() and getMin(), where getMin returns the smallest value currently on the stack, and every operation is O(1). Keeping one "current minimum" variable works for push (min = min(min, x)) but breaks on pop: if you pop the minimum, what was the minimum before it? You'd have to rescan the stack, which is O(n).

The insight is that a stack only ever changes at the top. While an entry sits on the stack, everything beneath it is frozen. So the minimum of "this entry and everything below it" is a fixed fact you can compute once, at push time, and store with the entry. Push x as the pair (x, min(x, min stored in the current top)). getMin reads the top pair's min. pop removes the top pair, and the new top already carries the minimum that was true before that push. Nothing is ever recomputed.

For example, push 5, 3, 7: the pairs are (5, 5), (3, 3), (7, 3). getMin is 3. Pop twice and the top is (5, 5), so getMin is 5, with no search. Duplicates are handled for free: pushing another 3 gives (3, 3), and popping it leaves the earlier (3, 3) underneath.

A common space-saving variant keeps a second stack that only gets a push when x is less than OR EQUAL to its top, and pops it only when the popped value equals its top. Using strictly less there is the classic bug: a duplicate minimum would then be lost on the first pop. Interviewers also like the follow-up "max stack" (same idea with max) and "min queue" (build a queue from two min stacks).

The harness runs the operations in order with their arguments ([x] for push, [] for the others) and returns the values produced by top and getMin calls only; pop is never called on an empty stack.

visualizationSteps.message: Each stack entry is a pair: the value, and the smallest value at or below it. Watch the min column -- it's what makes getMin O(1).
push 5: the stack was empty, so its min is just 5.
push 3: the min below is 5, so store (3, min 3).
push 7: the min below is 3, so store (7, min 3).
getMin: read the top entry's min: 3. No scan.
push 3: the min below is 3, so store (3, min 3).
pop removes 3. The new top already carries min 3 -- the minimum is restored without searching.
getMin: read the top entry's min: 3. No scan.
pop removes 7. The new top already carries min 3 -- the minimum is restored without searching.
pop removes 3. The new top already carries min 5 -- the minimum is restored without searching.
getMin: read the top entry's min: 5. No scan.
top: the top entry's value is 5.
Done. Pushing the duplicate 3 stored its own (3, min 3), so popping it left the earlier 3 still counted as the minimum.

recognitionSignals: A stack (or undo history) where you also need a running aggregate -- min, max -- after every push and pop, in O(1).
"Design a class" with an O(1) requirement on a query that would naturally need a scan.
gotchas: A single min variable can't be restored after popping the minimum -- the previous minimum has to be stored somewhere.
With the two-stack variant, push onto the min stack when x <= its top (not <), or duplicate minimums get dropped too early.
When the stack is empty, the first push's min is just x -- don't compare against a missing top.
confusableWith: Monotonic Stack: Find the Next Greater Element (this track) pops elements to keep the stack ordered, and discards data. A min stack keeps every element and never reorders; it just remembers an extra value per entry.
Stacks: Valid Parentheses (Fundamentals) is the plain stack this builds on.

complexity.note: Every operation touches only the top of the stack; each entry stores its value and the minimum at or below it, so n pushes use O(n) space.
